questions.question_text: A class wants to run a statistical inquiry about the school library. Which of these is a statistical question?

options.text: How many minutes does each Year $8$ student spend in the library in a week?
Is the school library a good place to study?
options.why: Asks for an opinion about the whole library, and no recorded measurement would settle it.

options.text: How many books does the school library hold?
options.why: Has one fixed answer that can be looked up, so nothing varies between individuals.

options.text: Should the library open at lunchtime every day?
options.why: Asks for a decision rather than naming something to be recorded from each student.

questions.solution_text:
A statistical question names what is recorded from each member and expects the answers to vary.
Minutes spent in the library differ from student to student and can be collected from each one.
**How many minutes does each Year $8$ student spend in the library in a week?**.

questions.question_text: An inquiry aims to find out how much fruit the students in Year $7$ eat in a day. Which statement is a hypothesis this inquiry can test?

options.text: Most Year $7$ students eat at least two pieces of fruit a day.
Eating fruit every day is better than eating none.
options.why: Judges which habit is better, which no count of fruit eaten could support or contradict.

options.text: The canteen should sell more fruit to Year $7$ students.
options.why: Recommends an action instead of predicting what the collected data will show.

options.text: Fruit is the healthiest food a student can eat.
options.why: Makes a claim about health, which is not the variable the inquiry records.

questions.solution_text:
A hypothesis predicts something the collected data can support or contradict.
Counting each Year $7$ student’s pieces of fruit shows directly whether most reach two or more.
**Most Year $7$ students eat at least two pieces of fruit a day**.

questions.question_text: An inquiry wants to know the mean age of the $1200$ trees in a town’s parks. The ages of $75$ of the trees are found from the town’s planting records. What is the population of this inquiry?

options.text: All $1200$ trees in the town’s parks
The $75$ trees whose ages were found
options.why: Names the sample, which is the part collected from, not the group the aim is about.

options.text: The town’s planting records
options.why: Names the source the data came from rather than the group being investigated.

options.text: All the trees in the town, including those in gardens
options.why: Widens the group beyond the parks the aim actually names.

questions.solution_text:
The population is the whole group the aim is about, and the aim is about the trees in the town’s parks.
The $75$ trees are the sample taken from that group.
**All $1200$ trees in the town’s parks**.

questions.question_text: An inquiry records, for each household in a street, the number of rooms in the house and whether the household recycles glass. Which describes these two variables?

options.text: Number of rooms is numerical; recycling glass is categorical
Number of rooms is categorical; recycling glass is numerical
options.why: Swaps the two types: a count is numerical and a yes/no answer sorts into groups.

options.text: Both variables are numerical
options.why: Treats a yes/no answer as a number because it can be counted up afterwards.

options.text: Both variables are categorical
options.why: Treats a count of rooms as a group name because the rooms come in whole numbers.

questions.solution_text:
A count of rooms is an amount recorded from each household, so it is numerical.
Whether the household recycles glass sorts households into a yes group and a no group, so it is categorical.
**Number of rooms is numerical; recycling glass is categorical**.

questions.question_text: An inquiry wants to know how many cars pass the school gate between $8$ am and $9$ am on a school day. Which collection method suits the variable?

options.text: Observation — stand at the gate and count each car that passes
Survey — ask students how many cars they think passed the gate
options.why: Collects estimates of the count instead of the count itself, so the numbers are guesses.

options.text: Measurement — measure the width of the road outside the gate
options.why: Measures a different quantity from the one the aim names.

options.text: Existing records — use the school’s roll of students who drive
options.why: Uses a record of a different group, since most passing cars are not driven by students.

questions.solution_text:
The variable is a count of events happening at a place and time, so the events must be watched and counted as they happen.
**Observation — stand at the gate and count each car that passes**.

questions.question_text: A class is planning the collection stage of an inquiry into how students get to school. Which step is an ethical requirement of the plan?

options.text: Tell students what the data is for and record their answers without names
Ask every student for their home address so distances can be checked
options.why: Collects identifying information the aim does not need, which puts participants at risk.

options.text: Publish each student’s response beside their name so the totals can be checked
options.why: Removes anonymity by letting any reader trace a response back to an individual.

options.text: Keep the purpose of the survey secret so answers are not influenced
options.why: Prevents informed consent, since participants cannot agree to a purpose they were not told.

questions.solution_text:
Participants must know what they are agreeing to, and their individual responses must not be identifiable.
**Tell students what the data is for and record their answers without names**.

questions.question_text:
An inquiry recorded the eye colour of $18$ students, in this order:
brown, blue, brown, green, blue, brown, brown, blue, green, brown, blue, brown, brown, green, blue, brown, blue, brown.
Which frequency table organises this data correctly?

options.text: Brown $9$, blue $6$, green $3$
Brown $8$, blue $6$, green $4$
options.why: Miscounts by tallying one brown response into the green row.

options.text: Brown $9$, blue $5$, green $3$
options.why: Loses one blue response, so the frequencies total $17$ instead of $18$.

options.text: Brown $6$, blue $9$, green $3$
options.why: Swaps the two largest frequencies between the brown and blue rows.

questions.solution_text:
Tally each response through the list in order, then count the tallies and check the total.
$\begin{array}{lc}\textbf{Eye colour}&\textbf{Frequency}\\ \hline \text{Brown}&9\\ \text{Blue}&6\\ \text{Green}&3\\ \hline \textbf{Total}&18\end{array}$

questions.question_text: An inquiry records, for each of $30$ Year $9$ students, the number of hours worked in a part-time job last week and the amount earned. The report must show how the two are related. Which display should be used?

options.text: A scatter plot of hours worked against amount earned
A dot plot of the hours worked
options.why: Displays only one of the two variables, so the pairing between them is lost.

options.text: A column graph of the amounts earned
options.why: Treats a numerical amount as a set of categories and still shows one variable only.

options.text: A sector graph of the hours worked
options.why: Shows shares of a whole, which suits categorical data rather than paired measurements.

questions.solution_text:
Two numerical variables are recorded from each student, and the aim is about how they change together.
Only a display that plots the pair from each student can show that.
**A scatter plot of hours worked against amount earned**.

options.text: The data supports the hypothesis, since $31$ of the $60$ students brought water
The data does not support the hypothesis, since water is only one of four categories
options.why: Judges the hypothesis by the number of categories instead of comparing $31$ with half of $60$.

options.text: The data supports the hypothesis, since water was brought more often than any other drink
options.why: Confirms water is the most common drink, which is a weaker claim than more than half.

options.text: The data does not support the hypothesis, since $31$ students is fewer than the $60$ surveyed
options.why: Compares the water count with the whole group rather than with half the group.

questions.solution_text:
Half of $60$ is $30$, so the hypothesis needs more than $30$ students bringing water.
The water column reaches $31$.
$31>30$
**The data supports the hypothesis, since $31$ of the $60$ students brought water**.

questions.question_text:
A statistical inquiry is carried out in these five stages, listed out of order.
**P** Collect the responses and organise them into a table.
**Q** State the aim and a hypothesis.
**R** Display the data and report the finding.
**S** Identify the population and the variable to be measured.
**T** Choose how the data will be collected and from whom.
Which order should be followed?

options.why: Names the population before the aim, but the aim is what decides which population applies.
Chooses the collection method before the variable it is supposed to measure is known.
Collects the data before deciding how it will be collected and from whom.

questions.solution_text:
The aim decides everything after it, the population and variable follow from the aim, the collection method follows from the variable, data can only be organised once it is collected, and the display and report come last.
**$Q$, $S$, $T$, $P$, $R$**.

options.text: The hypothesis holds for the class surveyed, but the sample is one class rather than all of Year $8$
The hypothesis holds for all of Year $8$, since $12$ of the $19$ students play at least two sports
options.why: Extends a result from one class to the whole year group that was never surveyed.

options.text: The hypothesis fails for the class surveyed, since only $6$ students play exactly two sports
options.why: Counts only the students at exactly two sports instead of two or more.

options.text: The hypothesis cannot be judged, since a dot plot does not suit the number of sports played
options.why: Rejects a dot plot, which is a correct display for one numerical variable.

questions.solution_text:
Students playing at least two sports are those at $2$, $3$, $4$ and $6$: $6+3+2+1=12$.
Half of $19$ is $9.5$, and $12>9.5$, so most of the students surveyed play at least two sports.
The hypothesis, however, is about all of Year $8$, while the data comes from one class only.
**The hypothesis holds for the class surveyed, but the sample is one class rather than all of Year $8$**.
